newsitem.title: FRANCE: Little sign of French truckers' strike widening.
newsitem.headline: Little sign of French truckers' strike widening.

text.p: Despite calls by some French union leaders to widen a 10-day-old truckers' strike to other sectors, there is little sign of the dispute turning into a broad labour revolt like last year's 24-day public sector strike.

Airline pilots began a two-day strike over their own working conditions on Wednesday, forcing state-owned Air France and its domestic subsidiary Air France Europe to cancel some flights, and rail workers in a single region staged a 24-hour stoppage.

But the unions are divided among themselves over whether to bring out other workers, and the fact that the truckers' dispute is in the private sector, rather than against the government, has limited any wider mobilisation, officials said.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe's centre-right government, has been working overtime to broker a deal between employers and the truck drivers, who have set up more than 200 roadblocks across the country.

Whereas last year the government was trying to reduce public employees' rights by making them work longer for a full pension -- a plan it eventually dropped -- this year it is dipping into the public purse to finance earlier retirement for the truckers.

After another marathon overnight negotiating session, government mediator Robert Cros reported agreement on Wednesday on two of the drivers' main demands -- early retirement at 55 instead of 60 and shorter working hours. He said he hoped to be able to conclude the talks when they resumed later in the day.
Even the Communist leader of the militant CGT union, Louis Viannet, acknowledged that progress in the talks had been largely the result of government efforts.

"Undoubtedly, there has been progress from the original proposals, but it must be recognised that this progress is based mainly on government efforts," he said on a visit to strikers on the barricades at Saint-Paul-sur-Mer in northern France.

"What I find scandalous is that before they even knew what the bosses' were prepared to offer, the government was already talking of easing their payroll taxes. In other words: the truck drivers strike and their bosses are given gifts," he said.
The CGT called a national action day in solidarity with the truckers on Wednesday, but apart from isolated demonstrations, such as by dockers in Marseille, few stoppages were reported.

The leader of another national union, Marc Blondel of Force Ouvriere (FO), who spearheaded last year's public transport strike, threatened on Tuesday to spread to the truckers' dispute to other transport sectors.

But Blondel, who bears a grudge against Juppe for ousting his union from lucrative control of the national health insurance fund after last year's strike, has relatively few troops and they do not seem keen to face new hardship.
The government last month postponed a potentially controversial reorganisation of the SNCF state railway, setting up a separate railtrack company, to avoid any risk of a strike.
And the country's biggest union, the Socialist-led CFDT, has ruled out widening the hauliers' strike to other sectors, saying the truckers would forfeit their widespread public support.

Political commentator Alain Duhamel said the fact that three-quarters of the public support the truckers, according to an opinion poll, did not mean they were ready to join the strike, even if it reflected widespread discontent.

Duhamel stressed the differences between this year's dispute in the thinly-unionised private sector, where a single category of workers were rebelling against working conditions widely acknowledged as harsh, and last year's revolt by more heavily unionised public employees with job security against a perceived attack in their long-standing rights.
